paras: The Napier Iron Works attack was a night assault in September 1881 by discharged white laborers on Black workers who had been hired in their place at the Napier Iron Works in Lawrence County, Tennessee. Accounts differed on its outcome: a Nashville report said a masked party severely beat a number of Black men, while another brief said the Black workers, who were armed, drove their attackers away. Tennessee papers described the conflict as a riot and a war between white and Black employees, and one brief called it a "race war."

According to the Nashville Banner, a number of white laborers at the Napier works had been removed and colored men employed in their stead. The Cleveland Weekly Herald gave the cause of the trouble as the employment of 25 Black men among the 100 laborers at the works.

The Banner, in an item reprinted from its issue of the 16th by the Milan Exchange, reported that a masked party of men visited the works on Wednesday night and "severely beat a number of negroes." The Banner named no victims and gave no number of attackers or injured.

A brief credited to the Conservator told the story differently, saying the discharged white men went to the homes of the colored men on Thursday night and "endeavored to mob them." In this version the colored men were armed and drove the assailants off, and the white men promised to return with fire-arms, "when a bloody time may be expected, if the threat is carried out."

A week after its first report, the Cleveland Weekly Herald wrote that the white and Black employees at the works were "at war" and that bloodshed was apprehended. No report of arrests, of the threatened armed return, or of any action by officials appears in the coverage.

The episode reached print mainly as one-sentence items in Tennessee state-news columns, the Milan Exchange's "Over the State" and the Cleveland Weekly Herald's "Facts and Fancies," which ran it between notes on crops, accidents and local elections. These items stated the hiring of Black laborers as the cause without comment, and the Banner's version called the victims "negroes."

Outside the state, the People's Advocate of Washington ran the Conservator's version on 24 September, placing it after a longer item on the whipping of a Black man at Adairville, Kentucky. That brief used the terms "colored" and "race war" and stressed that the Black workers had armed themselves and repelled the attack.

The Banner placed a completed beating at the works on a Wednesday night, while the Conservator placed a failed attempt at the workers' homes on a Thursday night. The Banner was a Tennessee paper reporting within days, whereas the Conservator brief carried no date, and the two may describe the same attack or two attacks on successive nights.

reader.title: Napier Iron Works attack
bases: Discharged white laborers attacked Black men hired in their place at an iron works, reported as a beating at the works (A3) or an attempted mobbing at their homes (A2), with the cause given as the employment of Black laborers (A1, A3).

Three apparently independent reports (the Nashville Banner via A3, the Conservator via A2, and the Cleveland Weekly Herald, A1 and A4) agree that white workers attacked Black workers over their employment in Lawrence County, though they differ on the day, the place and whether anyone was hurt.

accounts.label: Nashville Banner (via Milan Exchange)
accounts.gist: After white laborers at the Napier iron works were removed and colored men employed instead, a masked party visited the works Wednesday night and severely beat a number of negroes.

accounts.label: Conservator (via People's Advocate)
accounts.gist: Discharged white iron-workers went to the colored men's homes Thursday night to mob them, but the armed colored men drove them off; the whites promised to return with fire-arms.

accounts.label: Cleveland Weekly Herald
accounts.gist: A riot occurred at the Napier Iron works because 25 of 100 laborers were negroes; a week later the white and black employees were 'at war' and bloodshed was apprehended.

framing.detail: Tennessee papers ran one-line state-news items that gave the employment of Black laborers as the cause ('because 25 negroes out of 100 laborers are employed') without comment.
The People's Advocate, a Washington paper, reprinted the Conservator's 'race war' brief, which stressed that the colored men were armed and drove off their attackers.

versions.value: A masked party severely beat a number of negroes
Armed colored men drove the attackers off; a return with fire-arms was threatened

conflicts.note: The Banner account is a Tennessee paper's report dated the 16th; the Conservator brief is an undated reprint. They may describe one attack or two on successive nights.
Neither item gives a calendar date; the Banner's issue of the 16th points to Wednesday 14 September.
